title: Symbolism, Setting & Language
description: Swindon and London as contrasting theatrical spaces, the symbolism of Wellington, Sandy, and Toby,.
content_html:
Setting in a Play Without Realistic Scenery

In a conventional realistic play, setting is created through scenery, furniture, and props. Simon Stephens's play uses almost none of this. The graph-paper grid stage designed by Bunny Christie is the consistent environment throughout — it does not change when the action moves from Swindon to London. Instead, setting is created through lighting, projections, sound, and the movement of the ensemble. This theatrical choice means that the difference between Swindon and London is not shown through set changes but through how the stage feels: the pace of movement, the density of the ensemble, the quality of the light and sound.

For AO2 analysis, this means setting in the play is a theatrical construct rather than a realistic backdrop. When you write about how Stephens presents London or Swindon, you should focus on staging choices — how the production creates the feeling of each place — not just on what Swindon or London means thematically.

Swindon: The Known World

Swindon is Christopher's world: familiar, predictable, navigable. His home, his school, his routes between them. He knows the distances, the junctions, the colour of cars. Swindon represents a space of cognitive safety for Christopher — not because it is emotionally comfortable (it contains his father's lies and his mother's absence) but because he has mapped it, understood its patterns, and built his routines within it.

In the play's staging, Swindon is represented by relatively contained movement: the ensemble occupies predictable positions, the projections are of familiar domestic environments (the house, the street), and Christopher moves with confidence. The theatrical environment reflects Christopher's relationship to the space.

Key Fact

The same graph-paper stage represents both Swindon and London. The difference is created through staging: the pace and density of the ensemble, the quality of lighting and projection, and the movement choreography — not through realistic set changes.

London: Sensory Chaos and Independence

London is the play's space of maximum danger and maximum achievement. For Christopher, London is overwhelming: too many people, too many unpredictable stimuli, no familiar patterns to hold onto. The train journey to Paddington and the Underground sequence are the theatrical embodiment of this overload. Frantic Assembly's ensemble choreography creates a physical representation of the sensory world closing in on Christopher from every direction.

But London is also where Christopher proves what he can do. He navigates the Underground alone. He saves Toby from the tracks. He finds his mother's address. He travels further and copes with more than he — or the audience — knew he could. The play presents London not as simply hostile but as the testing ground where Christopher discovers his capability. The train journey to London is therefore the play's central symbolic sequence: it is where Swindon's safety is left behind and where Christopher's independence is forged.

The train journey is Christopher's literal and symbolic passage from dependence to independence. He has never travelled alone. The process of buying a ticket, navigating the station, boarding the train, and finding his mother's address is a journey from a child whose world is managed by adults to a fifteen-year-old who can manage his own. In theatrical terms, the ensemble's choreography of the train and Underground is the most complex and demanding staging in the play — reflecting the scale of what Christopher is attempting. His arrival in London is not triumphant: he is exhausted and overwhelmed. But he has done it. That fact — the achievement of arrival — transforms his understanding of what is possible.

Wellington: Death, Investigation, and Truth

Wellington the poodle is the play's inciting symbol. His death opens the action and gives Christopher's detective investigation its objective. But Wellington's symbolic significance extends beyond the murder mystery: he is the first link in the chain of hidden truths that the investigation uncovers. To find Wellington's killer, Christopher must discover the affair between his mother and Roger Shears, which leads him to the hidden letters, which leads him to understand that his mother is alive. Wellington's death is the key that unlocks everything.

Ed's killing of Wellington is also symbolically significant. He killed a dog — Mrs Shears's companion — in a moment of grief and rage when the relationship they had formed after Judy left him also collapsed. Wellington therefore represents collateral damage: an innocent creature caught in the wreckage of adult relationships. Ed's shame about killing Wellington is one of the reasons he maintains his lies: admitting he killed the dog would have forced him to explain why, and the explanation would have destroyed his version of reality.

Key Fact

Wellington's death opens the play and initiates the chain of discoveries. Ed killed him in rage and grief when his relationship with Mrs Shears ended — an act he concealed because admitting it would have unravelled his entire deception about Judy.

Sandy: Reparation and New Beginning

At the end of the play, Ed gives Christopher a golden retriever puppy called Sandy. This gift is carefully chosen: it is an animal, something Christopher can relate to without the complexity of human communication; it is a new life in place of a lost one (Wellington); and it is an act of love that does not claim to undo what Ed has done but offers something positive in its place.

Sandy cannot repair the damage of Ed's lies. The play is honest about this: Christopher and Ed's relationship is not simply restored. But Sandy represents the possibility of rebuilding: a new form of trust, created around a shared responsibility rather than around words. Ed understands Christopher's relationship to animals; this gift shows that he still knows his son, even after everything that has happened.

Language: Christopher's Precision and Others' Ambiguity

One of the play's central linguistic contrasts is between Christopher's precise, literal language and the ambiguous, metaphorical language of the adults around him. Christopher says: 'I find people confusing.' The primary reason is language: people say things they do not mean (metaphors, idioms, sarcasm, lies-of-omission) and expect others to decode the gap between literal meaning and intent. Christopher cannot do this. He takes everything literally.

Siobhan's language is the exception that proves the rule. She communicates precisely and unambiguously: she tells Christopher exactly what he is not allowed to do, and why. Her clear speech is the theatrical embodiment of what every relationship with Christopher requires — and what Ed, despite his love, consistently fails to provide.

In the play, Siobhan explains Christopher's difficulty with faces to the audience through her narration: she tells him that if you raise one eyebrow it can mean many different things — including 'I think what you said was very stupid'. This example, delivered through Siobhan's reading of Christopher's book, illustrates the problem of non-verbal communication for Christopher: a single physical gesture carries multiple possible meanings, none of them accessible to someone who reads only literal signals. The theatrical presentation of this in the play — Siobhan narrating while Christopher stands without recognising what she describes — is a precise theatrical image of the gap between Christopher's world and the neurotypical world around him.

The Symbolism of Mathematics

Mathematics is not just a subject Christopher studies — it is his primary language for engaging with certainty. 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' Mathematics offers Christopher what human communication cannot: rules that are consistent, proofs that are verifiable, answers that are definitively right or wrong. The play's engagement with mathematics — through the set design, projections, the staged exam, and the post-curtain scene — is therefore a sustained statement about what Christopher needs from the world: clarity, consistency, and demonstrable truth.

exam_tip_html: For setting, always write about how Stephens stages the difference between Swindon and London theatrically — not just what each place symbolises. For symbolism, connect each symbol to the play's themes: Wellington (hidden truth), Sandy (reparation), Toby (reliable relationship), the train (independence). For language, analyse the contrast between Christopher's precision and the adults' ambiguity — and how Siobhan's clear speech is the exception.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Swindon and London are represented on the same graph-paper stage — the difference is created through lighting, ensemble movement, and projection, not realistic scenery.
  • Wellington's death opens the investigation; Sandy's arrival at the end is a gesture of reparation. Both animals carry symbolic weight about truth, loss, and new beginnings.
  • Christopher's literal language contrasts with the ambiguous speech of adults around him — except Siobhan, whose precise communication is why Christopher trusts her.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use setting to explore the contrast between Swindon and London?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of how setting is created theatrically rather than realistically. Discusses: the graph-paper stage representing both spaces, the different staging in each (ensemble density, lighting, projections), what Swindon represents (cognitive safety, known patterns) and what London represents (sensory chaos and proving independence). AO2: theatrical staging choices as meaning-making.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with some theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response engaging with both settings.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the journey to London as the play's central symbolic event?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the journey as literal and symbolic: literal passage from dependence to independence, symbolic testing ground for Christopher's capability. Discusses staging (Frantic Assembly ensemble, choreography), Toby's rescue as a moment of courage under pressure, and the connection between the journey and the ending ('Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?').
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore the symbolism of animals in the play: Wellington, Toby, and Sandy.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of each animal's symbolic function. Wellington: the key that unlocks hidden truth; Ed's killing of Wellington as collateral damage and concealed shame. Toby: reliable relationship, companion in chaos, the Tube-rescue as courage. Sandy: reparation, new trust, Ed's gift on Christopher's own terms. Analyses how Stephens uses animals to embody abstract themes.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of at least two animals with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic discussion.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

knowledge_checks.q: How does the play represent the difference between Swindon and London without changing the set?
options: By using different coloured curtains for each location
By having Christopher describe each place in dialogue
Through lighting, ensemble movement, and projections — staging choices rather than scenery
Through a voice-over explanation before each scene

knowledge_checks.q: Sandy is a golden retriever puppy given to Christopher by Ed. What does Sandy symbolise?
options: A replacement for Wellington, symbolising forgiveness
Reparation — an act of love on Christopher's terms, not an attempt to undo the lies
Evidence that Ed is a good father who has changed

knowledge_checks.q: Christopher says: 'I find people _____.' — identifying his core difficulty with human interaction.
Christopher trusts Siobhan because she tells him exactly what he is _____ to do — precise, unambiguous communication.
Match each animal to its symbolic function in the play:
right: The key that unlocks hidden truth; his death initiates the chain of revelations
Reliable relationship and companion; rescued from the Underground tracks at great risk
A gesture of reparation — Ed's gift of new life and new trust on Christopher's own terms

flashcard_questions.q: How does the play create the feeling of being in Swindon vs London without changing the set?
flashcard_questions.a: Through lighting, ensemble choreography (denser and more chaotic for London), and video projections — staging choices, not scenic changes.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the train journey to London represent symbolically?
flashcard_questions.a: Christopher's passage from dependence to independence — the testing ground where he discovers what he can do alone in an overwhelming world.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Ed kill Wellington, and what does this reveal about him?
flashcard_questions.a: In rage and grief after his relationship with Mrs Shears ended. It reveals his emotional volatility and how much his concealment of this act underpins all his other deceptions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Sandy represent at the end of the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Reparation — Ed's act of love on Christopher's own terms. A new creature to care for, not a claim to have undone the past.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Christopher say 'I find people confusing'?
flashcard_questions.a: Because people's language is ambiguous — they use metaphors, idioms, and indirect communication that Christopher cannot decode. He reads only literal signals.

flashcard_questions.q: What example does Siobhan give about facial expressions and confusion?
flashcard_questions.a: She explains that raising one eyebrow can mean many things — including 'I think what you said was very stupid'. Christopher cannot read these non-verbal signals.

flashcard_questions.q: What does mathematics symbolise for Christopher?
flashcard_questions.a: His language of certainty — 'what is left when you have taken all the patterns away'. Mathematics offers consistent rules and verifiable answers that human communication cannot.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Siobhan's language unusual in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: She communicates precisely and unambiguously — telling Christopher exactly what he is not allowed to do. This makes her uniquely trustworthy to him, in contrast to all the.

glossary_terms.definition: In a non-realistic play, setting is created through lighting, staging, and ensemble movement rather than scenery — the play's Swindon and London are both represented on the same graph-paper stage.
An object, character, or event that represents something beyond its literal meaning — Wellington, Sandy, and Toby are symbolic as well as literal animals in the play.
Making amends for a wrong — Sandy is Ed's gesture of reparation: not claiming to undo the lies, but offering love in a form Christopher can receive.
Taking words at their exact face value, without reading figurative or implied meaning — Christopher's literal interpretation of language is central to his character.
Harm caused to those not directly involved in a conflict — Wellington is collateral damage in the wreckage of adult relationships around Christopher.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
The sense of anticipation or unease created by conflict, uncertainty, or approaching crisis in drama.
A recurring image, symbol, or idea in a text that carries thematic significance.
